title: Flexbox vs Grid
summary: Flexbox lays out one dimension at a time. Grid lays out rows and columns together.

rows.label: Dimensions
values: One axis at a time, row or column

rows.label: Sizing model
values: Track driven, the container defines the tracks

rows.label: Alignment
values: Along the main axis with justify, cross with align

rows.label: Overlap
values: Items can share the same cells

rows.label: Best for
values: Toolbars, rows of controls, equal-height items, centering
Page layout, dashboards, card galleries, magazine layouts

verdict: They are not competitors. Use Grid for the overall layout and Flexbox for distributing content inside a single row or column. A card gallery is Grid, the toolbar inside each card is Flexbox.

pickWhen.guidance: When you are arranging items along one axis and want them to size from their content.
When you know you need rows and columns, or want to place items precisely in a defined structure.

example.caption: A grid page shell with a flexbox toolbar inside the header.

commonMistakes: Using Flexbox with percentage widths when Grid tracks would express the layout directly
Forgetting flex-wrap, so items shrink instead of wrapping
Fighting min-width auto inside a flex item that contains overflowing content

title: The Cascade and Layers
summary: When rules conflict, the cascade decides the winner by origin, layer, specificity and order.
definition: The cascade is the algorithm that resolves conflicting declarations. It considers the origin and importance of the declaration, the layer it is in, its specificity, and finally the order it appears in the source.
explanation: Origin matters most. User agent styles lose to author styles, author styles lose to user styles when those are important, and animations and transitions sit in their own positions in the order.

Cascade layers let authors define their own ordering with @layer. Anything in a later layer wins regardless of specificity, which is how you keep utilities from being overridden by component styles without escalating specificity.
Inheritance is separate from the cascade. Inherited values only apply when no declaration targets the element, and inherit, initial and unset let you opt in or out explicitly.
keyPoints: Order of decision: origin and importance, layer, specificity, source order
Layers beat specificity for author level conflicts
Inheritance only fills in when nothing targets the element
!important inverts the cascade rather than simply winning

example.caption: Utilities in a later layer override component styles even with lower specificity.

title: Specificity
summary: A three-part score that decides which selector wins when two rules match the same element.
definition: Specificity ranks selectors by three components: the number of id selectors, the number of class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors, and the number of type and pseudo-element selectors. Higher components win before lower ones are compared.
explanation: The score is compared as a triple, not as a single number. One id beats any number of classes, no matter how many. Inline styles sit above all selectors, and !important sits above those.
The universal selector and combinators add nothing. :where() always adds zero, which makes it useful for zero-specificity defaults, while :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument.
Keeping specificity low and flat is the practical goal. A codebase where every rule is a single class is easy to override and reason about, which is why utility and layered approaches work so well.
keyPoints: Compared as three separate components, not summed
Inline styles outrank selectors
:where() contributes zero specificity
Avoid ids and !important in application styles

example.caption: The id rule wins despite the class rule appearing later.
example.code:
#title { color: red; }   /* 1,0,0 */
.title { color: blue; }  /* 0,1,0 */

:where(#title) { color: green; } /* 0,0,0 */

title: The Box Model
summary: Content, padding, border and margin, and the box-sizing decision that changes what width means.
definition: Every element is a box made of four layers: content, padding, border and margin. The box-sizing property decides whether width and height refer to the content box or the border box.
explanation: By default width applies to the content box, so adding padding or a border makes the rendered box larger than the declared width. This is the single most common layout surprise in CSS.
Setting box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border, so a declared width is the size you actually get. It is common to apply it to every element with the universal selector.
Margin can collapse between adjacent blocks and can be negative. Padding cannot be negative and does not collapse, which is why padding is the safer choice for spacing inside an element.
keyPoints: Default content-box adds padding and border on top of width
border-box makes width include padding and border
Vertical margins between siblings collapse to the larger value
Padding is never negative and never collapses

example.caption: Border box sizing makes the declared width the real rendered width.

title: Positioning
summary: static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky, and how each relates to its containing block.
definition: The position property changes how an element is laid out and what its offsets mean. The key idea is the containing block: absolute elements resolve offsets against the nearest positioned ancestor, fixed against the viewport, and sticky against their nearest scrolling ancestor.
explanation: relative keeps the element in normal flow but lets you offset it, and crucially makes it a containing block for absolutely positioned children. That pairing is the standard way to anchor a badge to a card.
absolute removes the element from flow and positions it against the nearest ancestor with a position other than static. If none exists, it resolves against the initial containing block.
fixed is positioned against the viewport, except when an ancestor creates a containing block through transform, filter or will-change, which is a frequent source of surprise.
sticky stays in flow and behaves relative until it crosses a threshold, then sticks. It only sticks within its parent, which is why it often stops earlier than expected.
keyPoints: absolute resolves against the nearest positioned ancestor
relative both offsets and establishes a containing block
transform on an ancestor breaks fixed positioning
sticky is constrained by its parent and needs a scroll offset

example.caption: The card is positioned, so the badge anchors to its top right corner.

title: Custom Properties
summary: Runtime variables that cascade and inherit, unlike preprocessor variables which are compile-time text.
definition: Custom properties, written with a double dash, are CSS values you define once and reuse. Because they are part of the cascade, they inherit and can be redefined per element or per media query at runtime.
explanation: Unlike a Sass variable, which is substituted at build time, a custom property is a live value resolved by the browser. Changing it on an ancestor updates every descendant that references it.
This is how theming works without duplicating rules: define the tokens on the root and override them under a media query or an attribute selector.
Fallbacks are built in through var(--name, fallback). Values can also be set from JavaScript with style.setProperty, which makes custom properties a bridge between styling and runtime state.
keyPoints: Resolved at runtime, not compiled away
They inherit and can be scoped to any element
var(--token, fallback) provides a default
Overriding on an ancestor re-themes the subtree

example.caption: The dark theme only redefines the tokens, everything else stays the same.

title: How do you center an element?
summary: Modern CSS centers in one or two lines with Grid or Flexbox. No more absolute positioning hacks.
shortAnswer: For centering an element inside its parent, use display: grid with place-items: center. For centering text, use text-align: center for the inline axis and align-content or an explicit line-height approach for the block axis. For centering an absolutely positioned element, use inset: 0 with margin: auto and a defined size.
explanation: place-items: center on a grid container centers both axes at once and works regardless of the child's size, which makes it the most reliable default.
Flexbox needs justify-content and align-items together, and behaves differently for a single child depending on flex-direction.
A fixed or absolute element can still be centered with inset: 0 and margin: auto as long as it has a definite width and height. Overlay dialogs often use exactly this.
keyPoints: Grid with place-items center is the simplest two-axis centering
Flexbox needs justify-content and align-items
inset auto margins center a sized absolute element
text-align center only handles the inline axis

example.caption: One line centers a child on both axes regardless of its size.

title: What is a stacking context?
summary: A local z-index arena. Some properties create one, and z-index only competes within the same context.
shortAnswer: A stacking context is a group of elements that are painted together and whose z-index values only compete with each other. It is created by the root element and by things like position with a z-index, opacity below one, transform, filter, isolation: isolate and will-change. A child cannot use z-index to escape the context it lives in.
explanation: This is why a high z-index on a modal can still appear behind a dropdown: the modal may be trapped inside a stacking context created by a transformed ancestor, so its z-index is only meaningful within that subtree.
The fix is usually structural, not a bigger number. Move the element to a higher level of the tree, or create a deliberate context with isolation: isolate where you want one.
Within a single context, painting order follows the stacking rules: backgrounds first, then positioned elements by z-index, then inline content and finally positioned descendants with higher z-index.
keyPoints: z-index only competes within one stacking context
transform, filter, opacity below 1 and will-change all create contexts
isolation: isolate creates one on purpose
A child cannot escape an ancestor's context with z-index

example.caption: The transformed card traps the tooltip, so its z-index cannot lift it above the nav.

followUps: Why does transform break fixed positioning and stacking?
How would you fix a modal that renders behind other content?

title: Collapsing margins
summary: Adjacent vertical margins merge into one, and a child's top margin can leak out of its parent.
scenario: You add a top margin to a child heading and the whole parent moves down instead, or two stacked sections show a gap of the larger margin rather than the sum.
problem: Adjacent vertical margins collapse. Between siblings the larger margin wins and is not added. Between a parent and its first or last child, if nothing separates them, the child's margin collapses through the parent and pushes the parent instead. Horizontal margins never collapse.

example.caption: The child's 2rem top margin collapses through, so the parent moves instead of the child sitting 2rem down.

fix: Break the adjacency. Adding padding, a border, overflow other than visible, or a display value that establishes a block formatting context on the parent stops the collapse. Using flex or grid containers also removes collapsing entirely, which is why modern layouts rarely hit it.
keyPoints: Only vertical margins collapse
Sibling margins take the larger value, not the sum
A parent and first child can collapse together
Flex and grid containers do not collapse margins

title: Responsive card grid without media queries
summary: Write a grid that fits as many cards per row as possible, with no breakpoints.
prompt: Write CSS for a card container that places as many 16rem cards as fit on the row, expands them to fill the remaining space, and wraps to fewer columns on narrow screens. Do not use media queries.
constraints: Cards should shrink and grow between 16rem and 1fr
hints: auto-fit and auto-fill control how empty tracks behave.
minmax lets a track shrink to a minimum and grow to fill.

explanation: auto-fit creates as many tracks as fit at the minimum size, then collapses empty tracks so the remaining ones stretch to fill the row.
auto-fill keeps the empty tracks, which leaves the last row left-aligned. Choose auto-fit when you want the cards to stretch, auto-fill when you want them to keep their size.
